name: Cylindrical Waves with Two Polarisations
description: Exact vacuum solutions describing gravitational waves with cylindrical wave fronts and both polarisations, the waves of Einstein and Rosen with the second polarisation switched on. The second polarisation makes the field equations nonlinear, and a wave passing through another has its plane of polarisation turned.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Einstein and Rosen's cylindrical waves carry a single polarisation, and their field equations reduce to the flat wave equation, which is linear [bicak2000]. On 11 November 1957 A. S. Kompaneets, at the Institute of Chemical Physics, submitted the case with the second polarisation let in, a term in the metric that couples the angle around the axis to the direction along it [kompaneets1958]. The equations he found are "two non-linear interacting cylindrical waves" [kompaneets1958]. Their characteristics are still the straight lines $x^1 = \pm x^4$ of his coordinates, which "shows that the strong gravitational waves propagate with a fundamental velocity equal to the speed of light, just as the weak ones do" [kompaneets1958]. Since the characteristics of each family never cross, he argued, the waves need not steepen into shocks, the fate of strong waves in a gas [kompaneets1958].¶Jürgen Ehlers, working in Pascual Jordan's group in Hamburg, found the same metric independently, with a trick like Guido Beck's applied to the stationary generalisation of Weyl's fields [bicak2000]. It appeared in 1960 in the treatise of Jordan, Ehlers, and Wolfgang Kundt on exact solutions of the field equations [jordan1960, bicak2000]. In the form named after Jordan, Ehlers, and Kompaneets the metric is $ds^2 = e^{2(\gamma - \psi)}(-c^2dt^2 + d\rho^2) + \rho^2e^{-2\psi}d\phi^2 + e^{2\psi}(dz + \omega\,d\phi)^2$, and the function $\omega$ carries the second polarisation [bicak2000]. With $\omega = 0$ it is Einstein and Rosen's metric again [bicak2000, halilsoy1988]. The two amplitudes $\psi$ and $\omega$ obey two wave equations coupled through $e^{4\psi}$ and through products of their derivatives, and $\gamma$ then follows from them by an integration [halilsoy1988].¶Where $\psi$ grows, lengths along the axis stretch by $e^{\psi}$ and circles around it shrink by $e^{-\psi}$, while $\omega$ tilts the direction along the axis toward the circles, the second, crossed polarisation [bicak2000]. Two such waves crossing each other turn each other's polarisation [piran1985, bronnikov2020]. When Tsvi Piran, Pedro Safier, and Richard Stark solved the equations numerically in 1985, they found "the usual cylindrical reflections and a rotation of the polarization vector of the waves", wherever the crossed polarisation is present [piran1985]. Piran and Safier called it a gravitational analogue of Faraday rotation, with one wave serving "as the medium for the other" [piransafier1985, bronnikov2020]. Shinya Tomizawa and Takashi Mishima built exact solitons of both polarisations in 2014 with Pomeransky's version of the inverse scattering method, and followed the turning of their polarisation along light rays [tomizawa2014]. They recount that in the solitons Akira Tomimatsu built in 1989, outgoing waves of the first polarisation leaving the axis turn wholly into the crossed polarisation where they meet the incoming waves [tomizawa2014].¶A single pulse of both polarisations can be written in closed form, and Tsvi Piran, Pedro Safier, and Joseph Katz did so in 1986 by applying the complex trick to Kerr's metric [piran1986]. The trick sends the time of Kerr's metric to $iz$, its coordinate along the axis to $it$, and its spin to $ia$, and two numbers survive: the width $a$ of the pulse and a strength $\alpha \geq 1$, with $\alpha = 1$ empty flat space [dinverno2000]. The pulse comes in from the far past, passes the axis, and goes out again, and it has no singularities [piran1986]. There is no conical singularity on the axis, and spacetime is Minkowski's in the far past and the far future [dinverno2000]. It is conical at spatial infinity, though, and $\omega$ grows without bound toward null infinity [dinverno2000].¶A standing Einstein-Rosen wave was Mustafa Halilsoy's seed in 1988, and from it he derived a standing wave carrying the second polarisation, written with Bessel functions [halilsoy1988, glod2022]. The complex change $t \to iz$, $\rho \to it$, $\phi \to iy$, $\omega \to -i\omega$ leaves the field equations unchanged, so that "any cylindrical solution has its cosmological counterpart", as Krzysztof Głód, Szymon Sikora, and Sebastian Szybka observed in 2022 [glod2022]. Halilsoy's wave becomes a universe of Gowdy's kind on the torus $T^3$, and in it they found evidence of "polarization gravitational standing waves", standing waves whose plane of polarisation turns from place to place along the wave's axis [glod2022].

related.text: The waves with one polarisation. With $\omega = 0$ the metric is Einstein and Rosen's, and $\psi$ obeys the linear wave equation of flat space [bicak2000].
Kerr's metric continued by $t \to iz$, $z \to it$, and $a \to ia$ and given new coordinates is the pulse of Piran, Safier and Katz, which has no singularities [piran1986, dinverno2000].

The same field equations on a torus in time. The complex change $t \to iz$, $\rho \to it$, $\phi \to iy$, $\omega \to -i\omega$ carries every cylindrical wave to a universe of Gowdy's kind, Halilsoy's standing wave to one on $T^3$ [glod2022].
The wave that stands still: with $\omega = 0$ and $\psi$ a multiple of $\ln\rho$ the metric is Levi-Civita's field of a line of mass [levicivita1919].
The waves gone quiet. With $\psi = \omega = \gamma = 0$, or $\alpha = 1$ in the pulse of Piran, Safier and Katz, the metric is Minkowski's in cylindrical coordinates [dinverno2000].
Belinski and Zakharov's inverse scattering builds cylindrical solitons with both polarisations, and Akira Tomimatsu followed the turning of their polarisation in 1989 [tomizawa2014].

coordinates.name: Cylindrical

parameters.description: Amplitude of the first polarisation, a dimensionless function of $t$ and $\rho$, with $e^{2\psi} = g_{zz}$; the spacetime is a vacuum exactly where $\partial_t^2\psi = \partial_\rho^2\psi + \partial_\rho\psi/\rho + e^{4\psi}\left(\left(\partial_t\omega\right)^2 - \left(\partial_\rho\omega\right)^2\right)/2\rho^2$, $\omega$ solves the equation beside it and $\gamma$ the two beside that

Amplitude of the second polarisation, a function of $t$ and $\rho$ with the dimensions of length, with $e^{2\psi}\omega = g_{\phi z}$, solving $\partial_t^2\omega = \partial_\rho^2\omega - \partial_\rho\omega/\rho + 4\left(\partial_\rho\psi\,\partial_\rho\omega - \partial_t\psi\,\partial_t\omega\right)$; with $\omega = 0$ the waves are Einstein and Rosen's

Dimensionless function of $t$ and $\rho$ fixed by $\psi$ and $\omega$ through $\partial_\rho\gamma = \rho\left(\left(\partial_\rho\psi\right)^2 + \left(\partial_t\psi\right)^2\right) + e^{4\psi}\left(\left(\partial_\rho\omega\right)^2 + \left(\partial_t\omega\right)^2\right)/4\rho$ and $\partial_t\gamma = 2\rho\,\partial_\rho\psi\,\partial_t\psi + e^{4\psi}\partial_\rho\omega\,\partial_t\omega/2\rho$, and zero on a regular axis

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \rho, \phi, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, $\rho$ a length fixed by $g_{\phi\phi}\,g_{zz} - g_{\phi z}^2 = \rho^2$, and $z$ a length along the axis. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, so $\partial_t\psi = c^{-1}\partial\psi/\partial t$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

parameters.description: Amplitude of the first polarisation, a dimensionless function of $u$ and $v$, with $e^{2\psi} = g_{zz}$; the spacetime is a vacuum exactly where $2(v - u)\,\partial_u\partial_v\psi = \partial_v\psi - \partial_u\psi + 4e^{4\psi}\partial_u\omega\,\partial_v\omega/(v - u)$, $\omega$ solves the equation beside it and $\gamma$ the two beside that

Amplitude of the second polarisation, a function of $u$ and $v$ with the dimensions of length, with $e^{2\psi}\omega = g_{\phi z}$, solving $2(v - u)\,\partial_u\partial_v\omega = \partial_u\omega - \partial_v\omega - 4(v - u)\left(\partial_u\psi\,\partial_v\omega + \partial_v\psi\,\partial_u\omega\right)$

Dimensionless function of $u$ and $v$ fixed by $\psi$ and $\omega$ through $\partial_u\gamma = -(v - u)\left(\partial_u\psi\right)^2 - e^{4\psi}\left(\partial_u\omega\right)^2/(v - u)$ and $\partial_v\gamma = (v - u)\left(\partial_v\psi\right)^2 + e^{4\psi}\left(\partial_v\omega\right)^2/(v - u)$, and zero on a regular axis

coordinates.convention: We use the retarded coordinate $u = ct - \rho$ and the advanced coordinate $v = ct + \rho$ of the cylindrical chart, both lengths, and $z$ a length along the axis. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
